,Below is a **step-by-step checklist** you can run on your workstation (Linux/macOS/Windows WSL) to:
1. **Make sure the file is a valid PMTiles archive** – no corruption, correct header, proper range-request layout.
2. **Discover the vector (or raster) layers that are inside** – the names you will use in `source-layer` in a MapLibre style.
3. **Optionally preview a single tile** so you can see the exact layer payload before you upload.

All of the commands use the **official `pmtiles` CLI** (the tiny Go binary) and a tiny Node script that leverages the `pmtiles` library + `@mapbox/vector-tile` to decode a tile. No extra server is required.

column1: You can also ask for a quick **human-readable summary**:
fields: { name: string, class: string, ref: string }
> * The **zoom range** (`minzoom`/`maxzoom`) that MapLibre will read automatically.
> * The **list of vector layers** (`id` values) that you can reference with `""source-layer"": ""water""` etc.
> * Any custom TileJSON fields you added (e.g. `attribution`, `vector_layers`).

If you **don’t see a `vector_layers` block**, the archive still works, but you’ll have to discover the layer names by reading a tile (next section). Some pipelines (e.g. raw `tippecanoe` without `--layer` flags) omit that metadata.
## 3️⃣ List layers when the TileJSON metadata is missing
The `pmtiles show` command only prints what is stored in the archive’s **metadata** field. If that field is empty, you can still extract a single tile and decode it locally.
### 3.1 Pull a tile with the CLI (no network needed)
# Grab the tile at z=0/x=0/y=0 (the root tile – it usually contains all layers)
*If the file is raster, the output will be a PNG/JPEG; for vector it’s an MVT (binary protobuf).*
### 3.2 Decode the MVT with a tiny Node script
// list-layers.js – prints the layer names inside an MVT file
That list is exactly what you will use in your MapLibre style’s `""source-layer""` property.

> **Why this works:** The MVT format stores a *dictionary* of layer names at the top of each tile. The first tile (z = 0) usually contains every layer that exists in the archive, so you only need to decode one tile.
## 4️⃣ Quick “preview” of a tile in the browser (optional)
If you want to see the geometry visually before you upload, you can spin up a **local static server** that serves the `.pmtiles` file and a tiny HTML page that registers the protocol.
# 1️⃣ Serve the file (any static server works)
# 2️⃣ Create preview.html (save in the same folder)
Open `http://localhost:8080/preview.html` in a browser. If the map renders, you know:
* The file is reachable via HTTP range requests.
* The layer names you used (`water`, `roads`, `buildings`) are correct.

If you get a **404** or **blank tiles**, double-check the CORS headers on the static server (the `serve` package adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` automatically, but some CDNs need you to configure it).

`pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles` → exit 0
`pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` – look at version, tile type, zoom range, bounds

Run a quick `curl -I -r 0-0 http://host/mydata.pmtiles` – you should see `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and a `206 Partial Content` response.
Same `curl -I` request from a different origin (or just load the preview page from a different port) – you need `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain).
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000` if the file will never change.
Ensure the TileJSON metadata (or your style) contains the required OSM/Overture attribution string.

Everything can be done with the **official `pmtiles` CLI** (or its Docker image) – no need for a running tile server.

## 2️⃣ Quick “is it a valid PMTiles file?” check
✅  All tile offsets are inside the file
If any line starts with `❌` the archive is corrupted – you’ll need to rebuild it (or run `pmtiles extract` to create a fresh copy).
## 3️⃣ Inspect the archive header – layers, zoom range, bounds, etc.

column3: Why it matters
`vector`, `raster` or `raster-dem`. Determines which `type:` you’ll use in the MapLibre style.
`minzoom` / `maxzoom` that MapLibre will read automatically when you use `url:` (not `tiles:`).
Geographic envelope; useful for splitting large archives later.
The exact `source-layer` names you’ll reference in your style (`""source-layer"": ""roads""` etc.).
Anything you stored with `pmtiles edit` (e.g. `attribution`). MapLibre does **not** read it automatically, but you can surface it in your UI.

column1: > **Note:** `pmtiles show` reads the *TileJSON* that is stored inside the archive header. If you generated the file with tippecanoe, Planetiler, or the Protomaps CLI, the `vector_layers` list will be present. If you don’t see a `Vector layers` section, the file is probably a **raster** archive (or the TileJSON was omitted – you can add it later with `pmtiles edit`).
## 4️⃣ Optional: Pull a single tile and decode it locally
This is handy if you want to be 100 % sure the geometry is readable, or you want to peek at the raw protobuf.
# Grab tile z=10, x=512, y=384 (replace with any tile you know exists)
Now decode it with any vector-tile library, e.g. **`@mapbox/vector-tile-js`** (Node) or **`vt2geojson`** (CLI).
You should see the same layer names that `pmtiles show` listed, plus a count of features in that particular tile. If the file is raster, the output will be a PNG/JPEG binary instead of a protobuf.
## 5️⃣ Quick “does the archive work over HTTP range?” test (local server)

Even though the CLI verifies the internal offsets, it’s good to confirm that a **static HTTP server** will honor range requests. The easiest way is to spin up a tiny Python server that supports `Range` (the built-in `http.server` does).
# In the folder that contains my-tiles.pmtiles
# Verify that we got something (should be ~1024 bytes)
If you get a **206 Partial Content** response and a non-zero file, the server is range-compatible. Most static hosts (S3, R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel) behave the same way.
